problem: Existing VLN instruction generators (Speaker-Follower, AutoVLN, ScaleVLN) are trained on small domain-specific datasets and translate local trajectories into step-by-step instructions. The output is low in diversity, lacks global context and high-level planning, and does not match how users state destinations or needs.
motivation: VLN models need massive training data, and manual annotation is too costly. Generated instructions should look like real user requests (brief destination descriptions or specific needs) rather than trajectory narrations. Models trained on prior generated data perform poorly on such instructions, which suggests a gap in semantic diversity.
key_idea: Build a hierarchical language scene description tree (instance/view/viewpoint/zone/scene) with an LLM, then have LLM-simulated user roles generate coarse demand instructions and refine them through top-down retrieval over the tree.
insight: Hierarchical tree retrieval gives much better training data than GraphRAG: on the 100-scene ablation, SR is 21.5 for NavRAG versus 12.1 for GraphRAG. Semantic and connectivity-aware zone partitioning beats distance-based hierarchical clustering (SR 16.4 vs 21.5). Models trained without user-role data drop on validation data that includes user demands (SR 18.6, versus 20.8 for the reverse setting), so instruction diversity matters. Models trained on AutoVLN and ScaleVLN data fail on NavRAG instructions (SR 16.2 and 17.4, with 10.3 for ScaleVLN R2R-style), which shows a diversity gap.
method: Navigation graph: builds HM3D navigation graphs for 800 scenes following ScaleVLN (dense sampling with 0.4m separation, agglomerative clustering at 1.0m, edges within 5.0m, max 5 edges per node). Also uses 61 train and 11 val MP3D scenes.
View/object annotation: samples 6 views (480x480) per viewpoint and uses GPT-4o-mini to describe each view, its objects, attributes and functionality.
Viewpoint annotation: an LLM aggregates view descriptions into a panoramic description covering area type, layout and object relations.

Zone partitioning: starts from the most-connected viewpoint and greedily adds adjacent viewpoints when an LLM judges they belong to the zone, updating the zone description each time. It then removes the zone's nodes and repeats.
Scene-level description: summarizes zone connectivity, zone types, functionality and a short summary.

User demand simulation: 20 manually written user profiles (age, gender, occupation, lifestyle). For each role the LLM writes 50 instructions issued to the agent over one day, using the scene description and previous records. This yields a rough instruction.
Hierarchical RAG refinement: the LLM picks the target zone, then viewpoint, then view top-down, and refines the rough instruction using the retrieved zone/viewpoint/view/instance text.
Data generation: 2,115,019 instructions over 861 scenes, 5 shortest-path trajectories per instruction (>10M trajectories), plus a NavRAG Val Unseen set of 7,396 pairs over 11 unseen scenes.

setting.backbone: DUET and HAMT (trained on NavRAG data); data generation uses GPT-4o-mini; LLM baselines NavGPT and MapGPT use GPT-4o-mini or Llama-3.1-8B
setting.training_data: NavRAG-generated 2.1M instructions over 861 scenes (10M+ trajectories) for pretraining, then fine-tuning on REVERIE without object boxes
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (6 views) at discrete nav-graph nodes
setting.simulator: Matterport3D simulator (discrete), with Habitat used for HM3D rendering and graph building
setting.privileged: none at test time (the fine-tuning setting removes REVERIE GT object bounding boxes)

results: DUET pretrained on NavRAG and fine-tuned on REVERIE without object boxes reaches SR 57.3 / SPL 42.0. This beats DUET pretrained on ScaleVLN (55.9 / 40.6) and AutoVLN (54.3 / 39.1) under the same no-object setting. Zero-shot on REVERIE val-unseen, NavRAG-trained DUET reaches SR 36.1, above MapGPT (30.2) and NavGPT (20.2).
limitations: No reliable way to evaluate correctness of generated instructions, since small human-annotated sets lack diversity and Bleu/SPICE/CIDEr comparisons are inadequate.
Targets are only viewpoint-level, so specific target objects and positions are not localized, which limits use in object-centered tasks like mobile manipulation.
Validated only in discrete environments; continuous-environment transfer is asserted but not tested.
